name: Bimaxillary osteotomy (bimax)

lead: Bimaxillary osteotomy, usually shortened to bimax, is an operation in which a surgeon cuts both the upper jaw (maxilla) and lower jaw (mandible) through the mouth, moves them to a new position and fixes them with plates and screws. In clinical practice it is used for bite problems such as underbites and overbites, for jaw-joint problems and for obstructive sleep apnoea.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as the surgical route to a more forward, balanced facial skeleton, often with a counter-clockwise rotation of the jaws. Published research supports it for bite and airway outcomes and reports high patient satisfaction with appearance, but formal evidence on purely cosmetic results is limited.

paras: Bone cuts allow the maxilla (typically with a Le Fort I osteotomy) and the mandible (typically with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy) to be moved forward, back, up, down or rotated. Orthodontic braces usually align the teeth before and after surgery, and 3D virtual planning is increasingly used to plan the movements.

Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection, temporary or permanent numbness of the lip and chin, temporomandibular joint problems, condylar resorption, relapse of the jaw position and the need for months of recovery and orthodontics. It is performed under general anaesthesia and is regulated as ordinary surgery in most countries; cosmetic-only indications are judged case by case by surgeons.

lead: Bimaxillary osteotomy, commonly called bimax or double-jaw surgery, is a form of orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery in which both the upper jaw and the lower jaw are cut, repositioned and fixed in a new position, usually through incisions inside the mouth.[1] It is used for bite discrepancies, jaw-joint problems, facial asymmetry and obstructive sleep apnoea, and is also sought by people who want to change facial proportions.[1][2]

Systematic reviews and trials around the procedure mostly examine planning methods, anaesthesia, pain control and blood loss rather than cosmetic outcomes.[3][4][5][6] One review of bimaxillary osteotomy for sleep apnoea reports sustained improvements in breathing measures and reports that many patients also describe a positive change in facial aesthetics.[2] Reported disadvantages include temporary or permanent sensory disturbance and a temporary restriction of jaw function.[2]

On forums such as looksmax.org the procedure is discussed alongside Le Fort I advancement, genioplasty, braces, implants and rhinoplasty as part of a larger facial-surgery plan, with frequent questions about insurance coverage, orthodontic preparation and surgery abroad.[7][8]

paras: In a bimaxillary osteotomy the maxilla and mandible are each divided by controlled bone cuts so that they can be moved as separate units and then stabilised with titanium plates and screws.[1] Orthognathic surgery in general is done to correct jaw mismatches in the front-to-back, vertical or side-to-side direction and can be used for airway, joint and aesthetic goals.[1]

The upper-jaw cut is usually a Le Fort I osteotomy and the lower-jaw cut is usually a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy; a chin procedure (genioplasty) may be added.[1][9] Combined upper and lower jaw advancement for sleep apnoea is also called maxillomandibular advancement.

Planning typically involves a team of oral and maxillofacial surgeons and orthodontists, with X-rays, photographs and 3D software used to predict the result.[1] Orthodontic preparation has traditionally taken up to a year, and newer approaches include surgery-first protocols and clear aligners.[1] Users on looksmax.org report that braces generally stay on through surgery and that orthodontic treatment is needed before and after a bimaxillary operation.[8]

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of virtual versus traditional surgical planning in bimaxillary osteotomy found that virtual planning shortened planning time significantly, while the difference in time spent in the operating room was not significant.[3] A 2025 retrospective study introduced a coefficient for measuring how closely bimaxillary advancement matches its virtual plan.[10]

General descriptions of orthognathic surgery say initial healing takes around two to six weeks, with complete bone healing taking a further two to four months, a mostly liquid or soft diet at first and swelling that can persist for weeks to months.[1] Older techniques wired the jaws shut for several weeks, while modern practice typically uses rigid fixation and avoids prolonged wiring.[1]

Human research on bimaxillary osteotomy is largely about technique and perioperative care. A systematic review concluded that deliberate hypotensive anaesthesia reduced blood loss, with serious organ-hypoperfusion consequences reported as uncommon.[4] Randomised trials have examined intravenous ibuprofen for preventive analgesia in patients planned for bimaxillary osteotomy and tranexamic acid for blood loss in orthognathic surgery.[5][6]

A systematic review of 76 studies covering about 3,400 patients examined the effect of orthognathic surgery on the temporomandibular joint and oral function; the authors reported that variation in techniques, examination methods and study design made conclusions difficult.[11] Older clinical series of Le Fort I and bimaxillary osteotomies in patients with open bite documented condylar remodelling and resorption, and a long-term evaluation described progressive condylar resorption after orthognathic surgery.[12][13]

A three-dimensional study of 44 patients, including 20 Class III patients treated by bimaxillary osteotomy, measured facial soft-tissue asymmetry before and up to six months after surgery.[14] A survey study examined which variables influence patients' perceived improvement and satisfaction after orthognathic surgery.[15] For sleep apnoea, a recent review reports improvements in apnoea-hypopnoea index, blood pressure and sleep architecture after bimaxillary osteotomy.[2]

Common reported adverse effects of orthognathic surgery include bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea and numbness caused by injury to the inferior alveolar nerve, which usually recovers over about three months, with permanent numbness described as rare.[1] A review of bimaxillary osteotomy for sleep apnoea lists temporary or permanent sensory disorders, a temporary reduction in oral-health quality of life and temporarily restricted lower-jaw function.[2]

Jaw-joint effects, condylar resorption and relapse of the jaw position are documented longer-term concerns.[11][12][13] Planning descriptions also mention psychological assessment to confirm that surgery is appropriate and to anticipate its effects.[1]

Forum members describe bimax as a bigger structural change than implants or chin surgery, and posts about it often cover counter-clockwise rotation, orthodontic requirements, insurance and travelling to another country for surgery.[7][8] Discussion of cost coverage frequently cites bite problems such as an underbite as the route to insurance funding, though policies differ by country and insurer.[7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, bimax is discussed as a major hard-tissue procedure, often in combination with other surgeries, with threads on insurance, braces and operating abroad.[7][8]

claims.claim: Bimax can be covered by insurance if there is a functional bite problem such as an underbite.
Braces are needed before and after bimax, and stay on during the operation.
Bimax with counter-clockwise rotation gives a better-looking profile than the same patient's current appearance suggests.
Bimax improves overall facial harmony and the airway at the same time.

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known jaw-correction cases.[1]
Hugo Obwegeser, with Trauner, is credited with the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy that underpins modern lower-jaw surgery.[9]
Rigid titanium plate fixation reduces the need for prolonged jaw immobilisation.[9]
3D imaging and computer-aided planning spread through orthognathic practice.[9]
A meta-analysis reports shorter planning time with virtual planning in bimaxillary osteotomy.[3]
